# What Your Character Knows

When your character attempts to recall information during play, your GM will call for an ability check. The difficulty reflects how specialized or obscure the knowledge is. This chapter tells you what your character actually knows at each level of that check.

**How to use this chapter:** Each category has three layers. Read the open text under each section heading now, before the campaign: it is baseline knowledge your character carries without effort.

The collapsibles below it are either *trait-gated* (open them only if your character has that proficiency, stat score, or role) or *check-gated* (open them when you succeed on the listed DC at the table). Do not read collapsibles for traits or checks your character does not have.

**What changes at each tier:** DC 13 gives you *facts*: the kind of thing a trained professional knows. DC 15 gives you *implications*: what those facts mean, what questions they raise, what a thoughtful person does with them. DC 17 gives you *dangerous knowledge*: what someone equipped with this information could do with it, and why most people are not told. These are three different kinds of knowing, not just three amounts of the same thing.

*Trait gates (proficiency / stat / role) appear under "What you know without a check." Check gates (DC 13–17) follow below each section.*


## Roman Military Lore

*Ability check: Intelligence (History)*

The Roman legion is the most effective military force in the world and you are part of it. You know this not from pride but from the daily experience of what the machine around you can do. You know the chain of command by reflex, the fort layout by muscle memory, and the names of the major Germanic defeats by the way veterans go quiet when someone brings them up. Three things every soldier knows without being taught: the Teutoburg Forest cost Rome three legions and the Emperor's sleep for the rest of his life; the Marcomanni have been pressing the Danube since before you enlisted; and the *aquila* -- the legion's eagle standard -- is never, under any circumstances, surrendered.

**What you know without a check:**

<details>
<summary><strong>History proficiency</strong></summary>

The three retired legion numbers (XVII, XVIII, XIX) and why they were never reused; the watchtower fire-signal code for your sector of the frontier.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>Athletics proficiency</strong></summary>

Formation timing by instinct -- you know when the line is about to break before it breaks; you can read a march's pace and know how many miles remain before the unit's legs give out.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>Strength 14+</strong></summary>

The weight of a full kit and how it distributes across the body after six hours; you can read a soldier's conditioning from across a courtyard by the way he moves under load.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>Optio role</strong></summary>

You command century-by-century coordination. You know what the centurion is about to order before he orders it because you have felt the line's condition. You read the temperature of discipline: when the right flank is getting tired (their spacing loosens first), when the left flank is holding too hard (the shields begin to tremble), when fear is spreading (it travels along the front line like ripples on water). A century without an optio is a century that dies when pressure increases, because there is no one to feel the line and adjust before the breaking point arrives.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>Tesserarius role</strong></summary>

You run the watch rotations and you know something no one else tracks: the mathematical point of maximum danger. A soldier who has been awake for 18 hours straight is no longer useful in formation. A relief that is late by 30 minutes can cost you a century. You know which months have the most attempted Germanic crossings: always when there is a new watch cycle and the timing is temporarily off. A commander who understands rotation schedules can predict Germanic attack windows, because the tribes have been watching the same patterns for eighteen months.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>Aquilifer role</strong></summary>

The eagle standard coordinates the legion in ways that voice commands cannot. When the legion moves, the eagle moves, and every soldier watches it from peripheral vision without thinking about it. A commanding officer gives an order but the eagle's position tells soldiers what he actually means. The eagle's movement language: a 45-degree shift means hold here despite pressure; a full retreat means full retreat, not a consolidation. The eagle speaks when officers cannot be heard in battle noise. When you carry it, you are speaking Mars's command language.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>DC 13 Intelligence (History) — Recalling standard legion structure, chain of command, and pay</strong></summary>

The Roman legion is organized in cohorts of roughly 480 men, divided into six centuries of 80 each. A century is commanded by a centurion; the first cohort of a legion is double-strength and contains its most experienced soldiers.

The chain of command runs: legionary (*miles*) to optio (centurion's second) to centurion to tribune to legate. The legate commands the entire legion and reports to the governor of the province, who reports to the Emperor.

The Germanic frontier has been active for most of the last two centuries. The disaster at Teutoburg Forest (9 AD) cost Rome three entire legions under Publius Quinctilius Varus. The Rhine and Danube rivers form the primary defensive line. The *Limes Germanicus* is the fortified road and watchtower system that supplements the rivers.

Current Emperor Marcus Aurelius has been personally campaigning on the Danube frontier for several years. The Marcomanni and Quadi tribes have pressed the Danube line hard. The situation is serious but not desperate, at least from the official dispatches.

Standard legion pay: around 300 *denarii* per year for a legionary, paid in three installments and subject to deductions for food, equipment, and burial fund.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>DC 15 Intelligence (History) — Recalling strategic context: frontier legions, foederati, and siege timescales</strong></summary>

The three legions lost at Teutoburg were XVII, XVIII, and XIX. Their numbers were retired permanently. Rome does not reuse the numbers of legions destroyed by barbarians.

The current frontier legions on the Danube include Legio XIV Gemina Martia Victrix, which has a distinguished history going back to the Boudicca suppression in Britain. Knowing which legions are stationed where, and their reputations, is useful information for political navigation at higher levels of military society.

The Marcomanni are Germanic, but they have significant trading relationships with Rome and are partly Romanized in their material culture. Their king, Ballomar, led a major incursion into Italy itself as recently as 170 AD — the first barbarian army to enter Italy in centuries, which caused considerable panic in Rome. The current campaign is partly about re-establishing the boundary after that incursion.

The *foederati* system: Rome pays certain Germanic tribes to fight as allies rather than enemies. These auxiliary troops are valuable and not entirely trustworthy. A soldier who understands this can navigate relations with allied tribes more effectively.

Siege logistics: a standard Roman siege of a fortified position required approximately one month of preparation for a serious fortification, assuming adequate supply lines. The party is not running a siege, but knowing the timescale changes how you think about strategic options.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>DC 17 Intelligence (History) — Recalling classified analysis: the Teutoburg parallel, the Emperor's hidden campaign goal, Germanic counter-tactics</strong></summary>

Arminius was one of us. That is the thing they do not put in the formal accounts of Teutoburg. He was a Roman-trained auxiliary, a man who ate at Roman tables, who knew the formations from the inside. The disaster was not a military failure in the field. It was an intelligence failure: Rome trusted a man it had made capable of destroying it. The lesson drawn was "never fully trust auxiliary leaders with tactical knowledge." The lesson not drawn was "the man most dangerous to us is the man we trained."

What this means now: Vercingetorix has been watching this fort for months. He knows its patrol schedule. He knows its weak points. He has not been educated by Rome, but he has been watching. The Teutoburg framework applies.

The second strategic goal of the Emperor's current campaign is not public: Marcus Aurelius wants to push the frontier north and create new provinces beyond the Danube. The Senate's opposition to this, led by Brutus's faction, is not simply conservative politics. It is a genuine strategic argument about whether Rome is overextended. Both sides are partially right. The party is living in the specific location where this argument has consequences.

Germanic tribes have learned to use Roman formation rigidity as a weapon. Lure the legions into broken ground or forest where the *acies triplex* cannot function. The forest beyond this fort is Germanic territory for a reason.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>DC 14 Athletics (Optio only — active: observing soldiers in formation before or during combat) — Reading the line before it breaks</strong></summary>

The century holds together until it does not, and the transition is measurable. Shield spacing closes by one foot when fear starts spreading. Breathing patterns change at the precise moment morale transitions from *can hold* to *cannot hold*. In combat, you can call out the moment when relief is needed with 90% accuracy before the line breaks. Use this: give the Optio player the information before the break occurs, and let them decide whether to act on it.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>DC 15 Intelligence (History) (Tesserarius only — active: analyzing the current watch rotation schedule) — The dawn vulnerability window</strong></summary>

The Germanic tribes have been watching this fort's watch rotation for eighteen months. Your relief changes are timed and your patrols are predictable. There is a 40-minute window each dawn when the northeast section is at skeleton crew: the overnight watch has not been fully relieved and the day watch has not fully formed up. The tribes will attack during that window. A watch officer who understands this can break the pattern before the tribes are ready. This check can only be made if the character has had access to the duty roster.

</details>

**Coronae — Military Crowns**

Military crowns (*coronae*) are the highest decoration a common soldier can earn. Unlike pay bonuses or land grants, a crown is a permanent mark of exceptional valor worn on the helmet at ceremonies.

- Every Roman soldier knows the three main crowns exist. A man wearing a Civic or Grass Crown is treated with visible deference even by senior officers.

<details>
<summary><strong>DC 13 Intelligence (History) — Recognizing a decorated veteran or asking what a crown signifies</strong></summary>

Three crowns matter to a legionary:

- **Grass Crown** (*corona graminea*): Woven from grass taken from the battlefield. Awarded only to the man whose actions saved an entire army or legion, usually an officer or general. The rarest decoration in the Roman world. A man wearing it has saved thousands of lives.
- **Civic Crown** (*corona civica*): Woven from oak leaves. Awarded to any soldier who saved the lives of his *contubernium* or century in a desperate action. A legionary can earn this.
- **Gold Crown** (*corona aurea*): Awarded to the first man over the walls in a storm assault, or for outstanding valor in open battle.

A man who has won one or more crowns earns permanent respect from any Roman citizen who recognizes them: small gestures (stepping aside, offering the better seat, not reporting a minor infraction) and more. The more crowns, the stronger the effect.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>DC 17 Intelligence (History) — Aquilifer or Signifer: the ceremonial weight of the eagle</strong></summary>

The Grass Crown is almost never given to a common soldier; but the *aquilifer* who saves the eagle from capture during a desperate retreat has been awarded it twice in recorded history. The eagle is the legion's soul: its loss means the legion must be reconstituted or disbanded in disgrace. The *aquilifer* wears a bearskin over his armor to identify himself, making him a target. Men who have held this role and kept the eagle alive are spoken of long after they are dead.

</details>


## Life on the March

*Ability checks: Wisdom (Survival), Strength (Athletics), Wisdom (Animal Handling)*

A march is not travel. It is a sustained physical system that either holds together or does not, and the difference between a unit that arrives ready and one that arrives degraded is entirely in the management of the bodies carrying the load. You know this the way you know how to breathe: it is not knowledge you recall, it is knowledge you inhabit. The pack on your back is 80 lbs of kit, food, and tools. You have carried it for six hours and you will carry it for six more. How you feel in the seventh hour depends entirely on what you did in the third.

**What you know without a check:**

<details>
<summary><strong>Survival proficiency</strong></summary>

Water sources by terrain type; the two-hour warning sign of incoming weather on the frontier (cloud formation over the hills before the pressure drop); which animals indicate safe foraging ground and which mean stay away; how far a column can march before horses need water (every four hours of march) versus men (every six hours under moderate load).

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>Athletics proficiency</strong></summary>

How long a soldier can run in full kit before becoming combat-ineffective (roughly 400 yards at combat pace); the maximum load a soldier can carry for 20 miles without degrading performance the next day (standard kit is 80 lbs, hard limit is 110 lbs before injury accumulates); how to identify a man whose legs are about to fail before he falls out of formation.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>Animal Handling proficiency</strong></summary>

The signs of a horse about to throw its rider; how to calm a pack animal spooked by combat noise; the difference between a horse that is tired and a horse that is injured in a way that will worsen with continued movement.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>Constitution 14+</strong></summary>

You know your own physical limits exactly: how much cold you can absorb before your hands stop working reliably, how many hours without sleep before your threat assessment becomes unreliable, the exact moment when you shift from tired to dangerous to yourself and others. You use this to manage your margin in the field, and you can read the same limits in the soldiers around you.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>DC 13 Wisdom (Survival) — Locating water, food, and shelter on the Germanic frontier in spring</strong></summary>

The frontier north of the Wall in April is early spring: ice in the mornings, mud by midday, cold nights. Water is abundant but contaminated at low points where animals and human settlement concentrate; clear running water on higher ground is safest. Foraging: young nettles (edible, nutritious), wood sorrel, early ramp (wild garlic), all identifiable. Dangerous: white-topped plants in damp ground (hemlock family); red berries in clusters before leaves open.

Shelter: Germanic longhouses in cleared areas may be abandoned rather than empty; they are warm but occupied territory. A shallow depression on the south side of a large boulder will be degrees warmer than the surrounding ground overnight. A spruce grove with dense canopy is warmer and drier than open forest at the same elevation.

Speed of assessment: a soldier with Survival proficiency can evaluate a campsite for water access, shelter quality, and defensive sightlines in under five minutes. Without proficiency, the same assessment takes 30 minutes and misses roughly half the relevant factors.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>DC 15 Wisdom (Survival) — Reading terrain for tactical advantage: where ambushes are laid, where a column is most vulnerable</strong></summary>

Germanic tribes prefer to attack at river crossings (ground is channeled, retreat is limited, footing is uncertain), at forest choke-points where roads narrow between treelines (the kill zone is pre-set), and at the bottom of descents where momentum carries a column into a prepared position before it can react. Flat, open terrain at noon carries almost no ambush risk. Dawn or dusk at any choke-point carries high risk.

You can read a road ahead for ambush probability from 300 yards if visibility is clear. The indicators: no bird activity in the tree line (birds don't flush if something has been still there long enough), broken vegetation at knee height on both sides of the road (someone moved through recently), a natural feature on one or both sides that would provide cover for a waiting warband.

The specific ambush position to avoid: the curve where a forest track bends and the following section cannot be seen until you round the bend. Germanic warriors favor the concave side of a bend in exactly the way Roman soldiers are trained to watch the convex side. They know what Roman doctrine teaches.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>DC 17 Wisdom (Survival) — Tracking a specific warband by their sign: composition, intent, and direction</strong></summary>

A warband leaves specific traces that tell you their composition and intent. Heavy boot pressure on the leading edge of each print: warriors at pace, not foragers. Disturbed bark on left-hand trees (a Germanic directional custom: left-side marks indicate territory entry, right-side marks indicate exit): this group was inbound, not returning. No fire sites visible along the route: either fast movement or they knew you would find this path.

A warband that moves without fire for two days is operating under one of two conditions: a *völva* has told them no fire (theological instruction, meaning a specific mission is in progress), or they are in a hurry and afraid of being located. Both mean they have a specific target. The composition tells you more: a group with one light print pattern among heavier ones has a scout element integrated with the main body. A group with uniform print depth has sent its scouts ahead separately, which means the scouts will be at the target before you arrive.

The useful calculation: how old is the trail? Compressed vegetation re-lifts at predictable rates in this climate; a trail in mud shows weather erosion after six to eight hours of rain. If you can estimate when they passed, you can estimate where they are now.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>DC 14 Strength (Athletics) — Arriving combat-ready after a forced march</strong></summary>

A standard military march covers 20 Roman miles in five hours. A forced march covers 30 miles in the same time but costs: arrive with legs compromised, first ten minutes of combat performance degraded (disadvantage on Strength (Athletics) checks for the opening engagement), recovery time roughly 30 minutes of rest.

A soldier who manages the transition can arrive ready: walk the last mile rather than run it; eat the remaining rations at the 25-mile mark rather than at the end; arrive with ten minutes of controlled breathing before contact. This is not common knowledge. Most soldiers run when told to run and fight when told to fight. The ones who arrive ready have learned the management through hard experience.

Mechanical note for the GM: a character with Athletics proficiency who declares forced march management as their action for the last mile of travel arrives without the disadvantage penalty. Characters without proficiency who declare it succeed on DC 14 Athletics or arrive degraded regardless.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>DC 16 Strength (Athletics) — Exceptional physical feats under field conditions: scaling walls, forcing doors, carrying a downed soldier</strong></summary>

Scaling a standard Roman fort wall (15 feet, smooth stone) without equipment: DC 18 Athletics. With a rope thrown from inside: DC 12. A damaged section with exposed stonework: DC 14. Fort walls are designed to be unscalable from outside and climbable from inside in emergency; if you know where the interior hand-holds are carved into the stone on the interior face, inside-to-outside is possible at DC 13. This interior knowledge requires having served at this specific fort for at least one season.

Carrying a downed soldier in full kit: 200 lbs or more with equipment. Counts as heavily loaded. You can carry them 30 feet per round at half movement speed. Athletics DC 12 to maintain for more than 5 rounds; DC 16 to run with them. On a failed check you drop to a walk; you do not drop the person.

Forcing a standard Roman gate under fire: the gate is designed to resist, not to be impenetrable. The weak point is the bar mechanism, not the planks. A character who knows this targets the bar housing rather than the door face, reducing the DC from 20 to 16.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>DC 13 Wisdom (Animal Handling) — Managing military horses and pack animals in stressful conditions</strong></summary>

Roman military horses are trained to tolerate battle noise, but specific triggers still cause problems: the smell of blood in quantity (not a few drops, but a freshly slaughtered animal or an active battlefield); sudden darkness after bright light; the specific sound of Germanic war-horns, which have a different timbre from Roman instruments and which the horses have not been systematically conditioned against.

Managing a spooked horse under fire: DC 13 Animal Handling, with disadvantage if you are also in combat. Success: the horse settles in one round and can be used normally. Failure: the horse bolts. DC 15 Athletics to stay mounted. On a failed Athletics check you are dismounted and the horse runs; it will stop within 300 feet if the initial panic stimulus is no longer present.

Pack mule versus warhorse response: mules are more stubborn and harder to spook initially, but once spooked they are significantly harder to calm than horses. A mule that has decided to stop stops. A mule that has decided to bolt bolts and does not respond to reins. Experienced handlers know not to apply sudden pressure to a mule that is on the edge; redirect rather than restrain.

</details>


## Roman Religion

*Ability check: Intelligence (History) or Wisdom (Insight)*

The gods are real and they are paying attention. You have known this since childhood. Roman religion is not primarily about belief; it is about maintenance. The relationship between mortals and gods is *do ut des*: I give so that you give. You make offerings, keep your vows, observe the correct festivals, and in return the gods hold up their end. When you sacrifice at the camp altar each morning, you are not performing a ritual for comfort; you are doing the practical work of keeping divine favor active. The Capitoline Triad -- Jupiter, Juno, and Minerva -- are the official gods of Rome. Mars is the god your unit actually prays to before combat. You never swear a false oath to Jupiter. The last soldier who did that in front of witnesses was found dead the following morning, and not one person in the century was surprised.

**What you know without a check:**

<details>
<summary><strong>Religion proficiency</strong></summary>

All twelve major gods by name and specific jurisdiction; which festivals require active observance versus passive acknowledgment; what constitutes a valid vow and what breaks one.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>Wisdom 14+</strong></summary>

You have noticed when the gods are paying attention. You know the difference between a bad omen and ambient misfortune. The feeling is physical: a change in pressure, a wrongness in the air. You may not be able to explain it but you have never been wrong when you have felt it.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>Sacerdos role</strong></summary>

The theological difference between state religion and private vows matters at the table. State sacrifices are formal, documented, and legally binding on the unit. Private vows are personal, undocumented, and binding on the soldier's soul alone. A soldier who has made a private vow to Mars in exchange for victory is a soldier who will not retreat under any circumstances, because retreat violates his vow. Tracking which soldiers have active private vows tells you which soldiers are most dangerous to use as a rearguard and most reliable as a first line. The Sacerdos is the only person soldiers tell about private vows.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>Signifer role</strong></summary>

Treason charges include automatic confiscation of the accused's property and redistribution to accusers and the treasury. This creates financial incentives for false accusations in Rome's legal system. A soldier who knows this understands that making an accusation against a wealthy officer is not just a legal act: it is a financial opportunity. The Signifer manages unit savings and knows exactly how much each officer's confiscated estate would be worth. This knowledge is dangerous. Use it carefully.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>DC 13 Intelligence (History) — Recalling the Roman pantheon, do ut des practice, and augury basics</strong></summary>

The twelve major gods of the Roman pantheon correspond roughly to the Greek Olympians: Jupiter (king of the gods, sky and thunder), Juno (queen, marriage and women), Mars (war), Venus (love and beauty), Mercury (messengers, travel, trade), Diana (hunting, moon), Apollo (sun, prophecy, music, healing), Minerva (wisdom and crafts), Neptune (sea), Vulcan (forge and fire), Ceres (grain and harvest), Bacchus (wine and revelry).

Additionally: Pluto governs the Underworld; Janus governs beginnings and doorways; Vesta governs the hearth and the sacred flame. The Vestal Virgins maintain the flame in Rome; if it goes out, it is considered a very bad omen.

Religious practice is primarily about maintaining good relations with the gods: *do ut des*, "I give so that you give." Offerings, prayers, and vows create and maintain divine relationships. Public religion (state sacrifices, temple festivals) is conducted by priests and magistrates. Private religion is conducted by the head of the household at the family shrine.

The *pontifex maximus*, the chief priest of Rome, is currently the Emperor himself. This is not unusual; emperors have held the title since Augustus.

Augury is the practice of reading divine will through signs: the flight patterns of birds, the appearance of sacrificial entrails, lightning, unusual events. The official augurs are a priestly college in Rome. In the field, the *haruspex* (reader of entrails) accompanies major military operations.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>DC 15 Intelligence (History) — Recalling the Mithras cult, sacra publica vs. privata, and festival calendar</strong></summary>

The Mithras cult (the *Mysterium Mithrae*) is widespread among soldiers and has been for about a century. It involves initiation rites, seven grades of membership, communal meals, and the central myth of Mithras slaying the primordial bull. It is exclusively male and particularly popular in the military because of its emphasis on brotherhood, courage, and the ordered cosmos. A Mithraeum (temple) can be found in most significant Roman military installations.

The difference between *sacra publica* (public rites, state religion, conducted on behalf of Rome) and *sacra privata* (private rites, conducted by individuals and families): both are religiously legitimate but socially different. Magic (*magia*) occupies a grey zone: some forms are tolerated; others are prosecuted. Love spells and curse tablets (*defixiones*) are common but officially frowned upon; spells against the Emperor or the state are capital offenses.

The Lemuria festival runs on May 9, 11, and 13 (odd days only). The head of household performs the black-bean ritual to appease lemures. During this period, temples are closed, marriages are avoided, and the general assumption is that the boundary between living and dead is thinner.

The Parentalia (February 13–21) honors the *manes*, the ancestral dead, with offerings at their tombs. The Feralia on February 21 is the public version. A Roman soldier far from home is supposed to observe these days even in the field; most soldiers do maintain some form of private ancestral observance.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>DC 17 Intelligence (Religion) — Recalling the devotio rite, the Sibylline Books, and why augury mechanics work</strong></summary>

There is a ritual called *devotio* still in the priestly records. A Roman commander consecrates himself and the enemy army to the infernal gods, then charges into the enemy alone, drawing their destruction down on both sides. It was last performed in the Samnite Wars. It has not been performed since because it requires both absolute certainty and absolute willingness to die. A character who understands this knows it remains available. They also know that if someone performs it and survives, something has gone wrong with the ritual, and the infernal gods will notice.

The Sibylline Books are held in Rome and consulted in specific crises. They have been consulted three times in living memory. Each time, the prescribed remedy involved Greek-style religious rites rather than Roman ones. Make of that what you will. There is a faction among Roman theologians that believes Roman religion borrowed its crisis tools from Greece because the Greek crisis tools work and the original Roman ones did not survive intact. Nobody says this out loud.

Technical augury: the *ex tripudiis* method (sacred chickens presented with grain before military action) is widely known. What is less known is why it works: the chickens are kept hungry enough that refusing to eat requires significant restraint. A chicken that will not eat when it is hungry is, in some meaningful sense, listening to something other than its hunger. The story of the general who threw the chickens overboard and then lost the battle catastrophically is the reason frontier soldiers take this seriously. He had decided the ritual was theater. The ritual did not share his opinion.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>DC 14 Intelligence (History) (Signifer only — active: evaluating the financial motive behind any accusation or counter-accusation in a political dispute) — The confiscation calculus</strong></summary>

Property confiscation from a convicted officer flows first to the treasury, then to accusers by a formula set in the Sullan proscription laws. A Signifer who knows the accused officer's financial standing can calculate whether an accusation is politically or financially motivated. On success: identify the financial motive clearly. On failure: you know the motive exists but cannot determine its size.

</details>


## Mars: Campaign-Specific Knowledge

*Ability check: Intelligence (Religion)*

You are a soldier serving on the Germanic frontier in the month of April. Mars is your patron god in the most literal professional sense. His month is March; his festival, the *Quinquatria*, was five weeks ago; your weapons were blessed in his name at the last *Armilustrium*. You do not worship Mars the way a civilian worships their household gods -- you serve under him the way you serve under a commanding officer. He is present in the impact of a pilum, in the discipline of formation, in the specific relief of still being alive after a hard day. The frontier soldiers who dismiss religion still observe the *Quinquatria*. They would not explain why. They simply do.

**What you know without a check:**

<details>
<summary><strong>Religion proficiency</strong></summary>

The exact words of the *Quinquatria* weapon blessing; the correct form of address when speaking to Mars before combat; the difference between Mars *Gradivus* (the marching god, god of disciplined war) and Mars *Ultor* (the avenger, the punitive aspect).

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>Soldier background</strong></summary>

What Mars's favor feels like inside a formation. You have fought in his name enough times to recognize when the ground changes under your feet; when the air thickens before a charge; when you know with certainty that the line will hold. Whether this is divine favor or battle-calm, you do not analyze it. You use it.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>Flamen Martialis role</strong></summary>

Mars on the frontier is not one god. He is three aspects: *Mars Protector* (of the fort's boundaries), *Mars Awakener* (of the warrior's clarity before battle), and *Mars Judge* (of whether a death was honorable or shameful). A soldier who prays to all three is not being redundant: he is acknowledging that Mars watches the same act differently depending on whether it is defensive, offensive, or conclusive. You perform all three rites before major operations. Most soldiers do not know there are three.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>Aquilifer role</strong></summary>

The eagle standard is Mars's material anchor point at Fort Vindolanda. When you carry it, you carry the god's attention concentrated into one object. This is not metaphor. Soldiers can feel it. The eagle is why men hold formation when they would otherwise break. The eagle is why a unit with no commanding officer can still function. The eagle is what Mars looks at when he judges whether the soldiers deserve his favor. The spear currently sealed in the vault is a second anchor point, older than the eagle, and they cannot coexist in the same space without one dominating the other.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>Haruspex role</strong></summary>

You read signs from Mars differently than from other gods. Jupiter speaks through patterns and omens. Mars speaks through blood and violence: the way a wound bleeds, the direction a spear falls, what animals refuse to eat or approach. The most accurate augury for Mars is to observe what he does *after* a violence, not what precedes it. A corpse tells you what Mars decided about that death. When the camp dogs all died the same night, that was Mars's verdict on what was sealed below. He was not cursing the camp. He was issuing a ruling.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>DC 13 Intelligence (Religion) — Recalling Mars's symbols, sacred month, and relationship to Rome's founding</strong></summary>

Mars is the Roman god of war and one of the three most important gods of the state, alongside Jupiter and Quirinus (the deified Romulus). He is the father of Romulus, the founder of Rome, which gives him a particular relationship with the Roman people that no other war god has.

His symbols: the spear, the wolf, the woodpecker. His sacred month is March (*Martius*). The *Campus Martius* in Rome (the Field of Mars) is where military exercises and political assemblies were traditionally held.

He responds to excellence in battle, not to random violence. A soldier who fights with discipline and skill honors Mars. A soldier who slaughters the defenseless does not. Mars is a god of war, not a god of massacre.

His sacred animals: the wolf (he sent a she-wolf to nurse Romulus and Remus) and the woodpecker (*picus*), which was considered a protective bird of the forest.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>DC 15 Intelligence (Religion) — Recalling Mars Gradivus vs. Ultor, the Salii and the ancilia, and Mars's relationship with Venus</strong></summary>

Mars has two aspects that practitioners distinguish: *Mars Gradivus* (Mars the marcher, the war-leader, the god of the legions advancing in disciplined formation) and *Mars Ultor* (Mars the Avenger, the punitive aspect, the god of righteous vengeance for wrongs done). His temple on the Capitoline was to Mars Ultor, built by Augustus to honor his vengeance for the assassination of Julius Caesar.

The *Salii*, the dancing priests of Mars, perform elaborate rituals in March involving the sacred shields (*ancilia*). One of these shields is said to have fallen from heaven as a gift from the gods; the others are copies made to protect the original from identification and theft. They are kept in the Temple of Mars.

Mars is closely associated with the founding of Rome and with the protection of Roman civilization against external threats. His anger is not arbitrary; it is specifically directed at threats to Roman order, Roman excellence, and Roman boundaries. When Roman soldiers fail to meet the standard he expects, he withdraws his protection. When they exceed it, his favor is tangible.

His relationship with Venus is complicated: they are lovers, which creates a divine intersection between war and beauty, between destruction and creation. This is not accidental in Roman theology; the two forces are understood as complementary.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>DC 17 Intelligence (Religion) — Recalling the spear in the Regia, the pignora imperii, and what it means that the vault spear is not the one in Rome</strong></summary>

There is a spear kept in the *Regia* in Rome -- the old royal house near the Forum, now the *pontifex maximus*'s administrative office. It is one of several *pignora imperii*, the sacred objects whose possession by Rome is considered bound to Rome's survival. The full list is not public: the shields of the Salii, the Palladium, the spear, and several others whose names are not written down. If one of these objects were corrupted or lost, the theological implications are serious enough that no one in the priestly college discusses them directly.

The spear you are looking at right now is not the one in Rome. What that means about this one -- who made it, what it was for, what it is owed -- is exactly the question you do not yet have the information to answer.

In older Roman religion, before the Republic, Mars protected fields as well as armies. The *ambarvalia* (the processional rite where farmers walked their field boundaries invoking Mars) survives as a trace of this. The older Mars did not distinguish between the violence of war and the violence of agriculture: clearing land, protecting borders, driving off disease. The frontier version of Mars, the one soldiers pray to out here where civilization ends, is closer to the original than the civic version in Rome. Out here, he is not a concept. He is a presence on the tree line.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>DC 13 Intelligence (Religion) (active: examining the relationship between the vault excavation and the subsequent omens) — What the omens are reporting</strong></summary>

The frontier boundaries are Mars's domain. The fort's east gate, the forest boundary, and any water that flows into the fort are his sacred points. The current excavation under the *principia* violated the east gate boundary without propitiation. The dogs died not as a curse but as a signal: the boundary violation has been registered. The omens (black livers, reversed birds, shadows without bodies) are not warnings of things to come. They are reports of what has already been broken. Understanding this changes what the party should do: the correct response is not to undo the excavation but to perform the propitiation that the excavation skipped.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>DC 16 Intelligence (Religion) (Flamen Martialis only — active: examining the spear in the altar chamber) — The contract terms</strong></summary>

The spear carries divine attention that will recruit whoever claims it, whether they consent or not. Taking the spear without the correct propitiation is not theft. It is accepting a contract with Mars that you did not read first. The contract terms are: use me in battle and I will make you formidable; become formidable and you will begin to need me; need me and you will never be able to set me down. A Flamen Martialis who understands this before the party takes the spear can potentially negotiate the terms. The window closes when the spear is first lifted from the altar.

</details>


## Germanic Tribes

*Ability check: Intelligence (History) or Wisdom (Insight)*

You are stationed on the Germanic frontier. You have opinions about the people on the other side of the palisade. Most of your opinions are wrong in ways that are useful to know. The Romans who die soonest on the frontier are the ones who assumed the Germans were just Romans without roads. They are not. They have their own logic, their own honor system, their own relationship with their gods -- and some of them know more about your fort's patrol schedule than your centurion does. The Teutoburg Forest disaster (9 AD, 160 years ago) cost Rome three legions. Soldiers still tell the story. The lesson is not that Germans are terrifying; the lesson is that a Roman who stops paying attention is already dead.

**What you know without a check:**

<details>
<summary><strong>Survival proficiency</strong></summary>

You can identify Germanic camp sign from Roman sign at 100 yards by smell and sound; you know which forest sounds are wrong (too quiet, the wrong birds, the specific silence before an ambush); you know which months raids increase and which months the forest goes quiet.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>Insight proficiency</strong></summary>

You read Germanic emotional register. You know the difference between a warrior who is afraid and one who is ready. You know what it looks like when a chief's authority over his men is slipping. You have been lied to by Germanics before and you know what that looks like too.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>DC 13 Intelligence (History) — Recalling Germanic tribal fragmentation, fighting style, and the chief-gift economy</strong></summary>

The Germanic peoples beyond the Rhine and Danube are not a unified nation. They are dozens of separate tribes with different leaders, different customs, and sometimes actively hostile relationships with each other. Treating "the Germans" as a single entity is a mistake that has cost Roman soldiers their lives.

The major tribal groupings the frontier soldier knows: the Marcomanni and Quadi (Danube frontier, the current main threat), the Cherusci (Rhine frontier, historically dangerous; Arminius was Cherusci), the Suebi (a broad grouping including many smaller tribes), and various coastal tribes of the far north.

Germanic warriors fight differently from Roman legionaries. They favor shock, speed, and ferocity over sustained formation combat. They are not disciplined in the Roman sense; their power comes from individual excellence (*virtus* exists in German culture, though called by different names) and the bonds of the war-band (*comitatus*). They fight best in forest, ambush, broken ground. They struggle against disciplined infantry in open formation.

Germanic chiefs command loyalty through demonstrated personal excellence and through gift-giving. A chief who cannot give gifts loses followers. Raiding Roman territory is partly about demonstrating that the chief can provide.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>DC 15 Intelligence (History) or Wisdom (Insight) — Recalling the comitatus system, the Thing, wergild law, and sacred bog sites</strong></summary>

The *comitatus* is the Germanic war-band structure: a chief surrounded by warrior companions who have personally sworn loyalty to him. The bond is personal and mutual; the chief owes the companions equipment, food, and share of plunder; the companions owe him their lives. A companion who outlives his chief in battle has failed fundamentally; this is not abstract shame but concrete social destruction.

This means that killing the chief in battle is often more decisive than killing half his warriors. The warriors of the *comitatus* may scatter or even switch sides after a chief's death, because their oath was personal, not institutional.

The *Thing* is the Germanic assembly where free men gather to make decisions, resolve disputes through law-speaking, and witness oaths. It has real authority; even a powerful chief cannot simply override a Thing's decision without losing face and followers. This is the closest thing Germanic society has to republican governance.

*Wergild* (blood price): Germanic law resolves most inter-personal violence through payment rather than punishment. Every free person has a *wergild* value; if you kill them, you pay their family that value or the family has the right to feud. A Roman soldier who understands this can resolve a killing that might otherwise escalate into a cycle of violence.

Germanic religious sites are primarily natural: sacred groves, specific rivers, notable trees, bogs. The bog is particularly significant; offerings (including human sacrifices in specific circumstances) are made there. A Roman entering a sacred site without acknowledgment is committing an offense that the tribe will notice.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>DC 17 Intelligence (History) — Recalling Germanic battle-death theology, Tacitus's limits, and the völva's true social category</strong></summary>

Germanic warriors seek battle-death on purpose. This is not nihilism. In their cosmology, warriors who die in battle go to the hall of the war-god; those who die otherwise go to a grey realm. They are not being reckless when they charge without regard for their lives. They are making a theological choice. A Roman officer who understands this knows that you cannot make Germanic warriors afraid of dying. You can only make them respect you, or give up on converting them into a position of defeat that does not honor the choice they have made.

Tacitus wrote a detailed account of the Germanic peoples roughly a century ago. It is biased: he used the Germans as a mirror to criticize Roman decadence, which means he idealized things he found convenient to idealize. It is still useful, because the parts he was not using rhetorically tend to be accurate.

The woman you are looking for -- the *volva*, the staff-carrier -- exists outside normal social categories in ways Rome does not have a clean equivalent for. She is not a priestess. She is not a wife or a slave. She travels, she performs ritual, she gives judgments that war-leaders cannot contradict publicly without losing followers. The war-god learned her art from the goddess of the dead, in the Germanic tradition: this is considered a source of both power and cost for both of them. A Roman who treats her as a curiosity has misread the room completely. Treat her as you would treat a senior augur with the backing of an army she does not show you.

Germanic runes are not decoration. Carving a rune correctly is also an act of invocation. Whether this is literally true is something you will have your own view on by the end of this campaign.

</details>


## The Frontier

*Ability check: Intelligence (History) or Wisdom (Survival)*

The frontier is not where Rome ends. It is where you are. You know the *Limes* the way you know the calluses on your palms: in exhaustive, functional detail. You know which watchtower has the loose bottom step, which section of road floods in spring, which stretch of forest smells different because the trees are wrong -- too dense, too dark, no birdsong. The traders who cross legally bring grain, amber, furs, and information. The ones who cross without authorization bring problems. A soldier who crosses without orders brings a court martial and, if he is unlucky, a cross. The line between here and there is not philosophical. It is a ditch, a palisade, and a watchfire, and everything beyond it is actively trying to read your patrol schedule.

**What you know without a check:**

<details>
<summary><strong>Survival proficiency</strong></summary>

The monthly pattern of raid activity in your sector; how to read your sector's fire-signal system without thinking about it; what a ford looks like at 400 yards in low visibility; the tree-line anomalies that precede an ambush at three of the most common approach points.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>Perception proficiency</strong></summary>

You notice what does not belong. A track that goes in without coming out. A tree blazed in a pattern that is not Roman military marking. Smoke from the wrong direction. You cannot always say what it means but you always notice it.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>DC 13 Intelligence (History) or Wisdom (Survival) — Recalling the Limes system, raid response doctrine, and fire-signal codes</strong></summary>

The Rhine and Danube rivers form the primary Roman defensive line in northern Europe. The *Limes Germanicus* supplements this with a system of roads, watchtowers, and fortified posts that parallels the rivers through territory that is not always defensible from the rivers alone.

The territory beyond the frontier is called *Germania Magna* (Greater Germania) and is not under Roman control, though traders cross regularly and Rome has significant intelligence about conditions there. The forests are denser than anything in the Romanized world; Roman military doctrine has never worked well in them.

The fortified watchtowers (*burgi*) signal by fire: one fire for all clear, two for alert, patterns for specific threat types. Every soldier on the frontier knows the basic signal code for their sector. Communication between posts takes approximately one hour per twelve miles under good conditions.

Germanic raids on the Roman side of the frontier happen regularly. They are not always full military operations; often they are cattle raids, opportunistic looting, or demonstrations of a chief's power. The Roman response is supposed to be fast, proportionate, and visible. A response that is too slow encourages more raids; a response that is disproportionate inflames the tribes and can trigger larger conflicts.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>DC 15 Wisdom (Survival) — Recalling forest navigation, vicus intelligence value, river crossing vulnerability, and seasonal raid patterns</strong></summary>

The Germanic forest is genuinely different from Roman-managed woodland. Old-growth forest in the Hercynian region (the great forest of central Europe) is dark at midday, has almost no undergrowth in places (the canopy is too dense), and supports wildlife that has not learned to fear humans because humans rarely enter. Navigation is by landmark and sun when visible, not by track.

The frontier trading posts (*vici*) that grow up outside Roman forts are sources of intelligence as well as commerce. Germanic traders bring information about conditions across the frontier, often without intending to. A soldier who knows how to listen to market gossip, who knows what goods moving in what direction indicate about internal tribal politics, has a significant information advantage.

River crossings are the most vulnerable point of any frontier operation in both directions. The Rhine and Danube are broad and cold; unassisted crossing takes time and leaves troops exposed. Germanic forces know this and frequently target crossing operations. The position of known fords is strategic information.

Seasonal patterns of Germanic activity: raids are most common in summer (better weather, easier movement) and sometimes in early winter (before the deep freeze, while food stores can still be taken). Deep winter on the frontier is quiet. Spring is when movements begin again; the period of maximum uncertainty.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>DC 17 Intelligence (History) — Recalling the frumentarii network, the population-growth strategic problem, and Rome's active management of Germanic politics</strong></summary>

The *frumentarii* are officially grain-supply officers. They are not grain-supply officers. They are the closest thing Rome has to a secret service, and they maintain informants on both sides of this frontier. If you know how to signal the network, you can sometimes access information that would not otherwise be available. If you do not know how to signal it, you might walk past an informant three times a week without knowing it.

The long-term strategic picture that nobody says plainly in official dispatches: the Germanic population is growing and the Roman frontier population is not. This has been in the internal reports for two generations. Marcus Aurelius's plan to push the frontier north is one proposed answer. Brutus's faction in the Senate has a different proposed answer: accept a shorter frontier and defend it more tightly. Both positions are responses to the same underlying fact. You are standing in the location where that political argument has physical consequences.

Rome manages Germanic internal politics actively: subsidizing friendly chiefs, undermining hostile ones, controlling trade access as leverage. A chief who raids Rome loses trading relationships; a chief who cooperates gains status gifts that make him powerful without him fully controlling where his power comes from. This mechanism works both ways. A character who understands it can move within it -- including finding the specific chiefs around this fort who are being subsidized by someone whose interests are not Rome's.

</details>


## Roman Law and Politics

*Ability check: Intelligence (History)*

You know less about the Senate than you think you do, and more than a civilian would. You know that the Emperor holds his power through the army, the Senate, and the grace of the gods, roughly in that order. You know that a Triumph is real -- you may have witnessed one -- and that the right to hold one is a formal declaration tied to specific military achievements, not an automatic grant. You know what treason means in practical terms: you said something wrong in front of someone who remembered it. The law exists, it is real, and it applies to soldiers as well as senators. What you do not know, and should not pretend to know, is what goes on inside the Curia on any given afternoon. The Senate is not your world. It affects your world. That is a meaningful distinction.

**What you know without a check:**

<details>
<summary><strong>History proficiency</strong></summary>

The current consuls by name (Lucius Fulvius Rufus and Marcus Plautius Quintillus, in the year of the campaign); what *damnatio memoriae* is and the last major figure it was applied to; the basic structure of a senatorial trial.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>Noble background</strong></summary>

The Senate's current principal factions and their positions on the frontier war; Senator Brutus's public reputation as a conservative reformer and his documented opposition to the Emperor's Danube expansion policy; which senatorial families have frontier interests and which consider it an expensive distraction.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>DC 13 Intelligence (History) — Recalling Roman government structure, the Emperor's authority, and treason law</strong></summary>

Rome is governed by the Emperor, the Senate, and a complex of magistracies (consul, praetor, quaestor, aedile, tribune of the plebs). In practical terms, the Emperor holds supreme executive, military, and increasingly judicial authority; the Senate retains significant prestige and some legislative function; the magistracies still operate but largely within the Emperor's framework.

The Senate consists of approximately 600 men of senatorial rank. Membership is hereditary but can be granted or removed. Senators are supposed to be wealthy landowners from Italy, though in practice the Senate has been opened to provincial elites over the centuries. A senator from Africa or Spain is not unusual.

The Emperor in 175 AD is Marcus Aurelius Antoninus Augustus, now in his early fifties. He is known as a Stoic philosopher and has published personal reflections (the *Meditations*) that circulate among educated Romans. He is generally respected, sometimes idealized, and has been on campaign for most of the last decade. His co-emperor Lucius Verus died in 169 AD.

Treason (*perduellio* or *maiestas*) is the most serious political crime. The charge can cover a wide range of offenses: actual conspiracy against the Emperor, public defamation of the Emperor, failure to prosecute a known traitor. Conviction generally meant death and forfeiture of all property. Accusers were sometimes rewarded from the convicted person's estate, which created obvious incentives for false accusation.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>DC 15 Intelligence (History) — Recalling the Triumph, Senate factions, the Praetorian Guard, and treason trial procedure</strong></summary>

A Triumph is the highest military honor Rome can grant: a formal procession through Rome in which the victorious general, dressed as Jupiter, rides in a chariot from the Capitoline Hill through the Forum. The Senate must grant permission for a Triumph; the conditions include a significant foreign victory and a minimum number of enemy killed. The Emperor is currently due a Triumph for his Danube victories; the date and processional route have been announced.

The Senate's factions in 175 AD: broadly, there are those who support the Emperor's expansive frontier policy (more provinces, more glory, more territory) and those who oppose it (overextension, expense, distraction from internal problems). Brutus's faction is the latter: they want a negotiated boundary, reduced military spending, and restored senatorial authority. This is not an irrational position; it has serious historical and financial arguments behind it.

The Praetorian Guard: the Emperor's personal bodyguard, stationed in Rome and commanded by Praetorian Prefects. They are better paid than legionary soldiers and considerably better connected politically. Historically, they have been kingmakers in moments of political crisis. In 175 AD they are loyal to Marcus Aurelius, but their loyalty is institutional, not personal; they would transfer it smoothly to a successor.

Legal procedure for treason charges: accusation, formal arrest, Senate trial (for senators), or imperial court (for others). The accused has the right to speak in their defense. Evidence matters. Witnesses matter. A well-organized case with credible witnesses and documentary evidence is significantly more likely to succeed than a bare accusation.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>DC 17 Intelligence (History) — Recalling damnatio memoriae, the constitutional path to bring down a senator, and what the party needs for Session 5</strong></summary>

*Damnatio memoriae* -- condemnation of memory. The Senate can vote to erase a convicted traitor from the record. Statues come down. Names are chiseled off inscriptions. The name is not spoken at public occasions. It has happened to emperors. It can happen to a senator. For someone like Brutus, who is in the business of being remembered, who has spent his career constructing a legacy worth inheriting -- this is a worse outcome than death. He knows this. It is the one thing that might reach him when nothing else does.

The mechanism for bringing a senator down through Roman law is available but requires specific pieces: evidence presentable in a formal proceeding, at least one credible witness willing to testify publicly, and access to either the Senate itself or the Emperor's direct judicial authority. A Praetorian arrest without prior senatorial consent is constitutionally irregular and creates political risk for whoever orders it. This is not impossible; it is just complicated enough that Brutus has calculated nobody will attempt it while he controls the narrative.

If the party reaches Session 5 with evidence, a witness, and some form of imperial access -- they have a path that does not require killing him. Whether they want to take it is a different question.

</details>


## Roman Military Authority

*Ability checks: Charisma (Intimidation), Charisma (Persuasion), Charisma (Performance)*

Command is a physical act before it is a social one. The centurion's voice that carries 200 yards across a battlefield without shouting is not a gift. It is a technique, built over years of standing in front of men and being responsible for whether they live or die. You know which end of authority you occupy. You know how to give an order that will be followed and how to give one that will be quietly ignored. You also know that rank alone does not produce obedience on the frontier: the soldiers here have seen enough to know the difference between an officer who knows what he is doing and one who does not. They follow the former. The latter they protect from their own incompetence, which is not the same thing.

**What you know without a check:**

<details>
<summary><strong>Intimidation proficiency</strong></summary>

The specific display behaviors that Roman military authority uses: the parade-ground voice that carries without shouting; the body language of a soldier who has given the last warning; the difference between Germanic warriors who are testing your resolve (they respond to escalation) and those who are committed to contact (escalation makes it worse, not better).

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>Persuasion proficiency</strong></summary>

The social hierarchy of the frontier and who can authorize what: what a decurion can authorize, what requires a centurion, what requires the Legate; how to frame a request to avoid triggering rank-protectionism; which NPCs in the fort respond to military formality and which respond to direct personal appeal.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>Performance proficiency</strong></summary>

Military ceremony functions as battlefield Intimidation at scale. The *testudo* formation is not only a tactic; it is a performance. A unit that moves with military precision has advantage on group Intimidation checks against opponents who understand what they are seeing. Germanic warriors specifically recognize Roman formation discipline, and some will break before contact if it is displayed correctly and consistently.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>DC 13 Charisma (Intimidation) — Establishing military authority over undisciplined elements in a crisis</strong></summary>

Roman military rank is a physical fact: uniform, bearing, and command voice create authority that most people inside the Roman system respond to without thinking, even if you are a lower rank than the person you are commanding. The technique has three components: give the order without hesitation, use specific actionable language ("Move to the wall," not "We should probably consider moving"), and do not acknowledge resistance verbally. Resistance that is acknowledged has been given legitimacy it did not have before.

DC thresholds: DC 13 Charisma (Intimidation) to override civilian resistance in a crisis. DC 15 to override a soldier of equal rank who has a conflicting order. DC 17 to override a superior who has already given a conflicting order and is present. The last option succeeds or fails publicly; there is no quiet version of overriding a superior's order in front of witnesses.

Failure consequence: the person does not comply, and they now know you tried and failed. Subsequent attempts in the same encounter increase in DC by 2.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>DC 15 Charisma (Persuasion) — Extracting information from an NPC who is afraid to speak</strong></summary>

A person who has information and is afraid to give it is afraid of a specific consequence. Identifying the consequence and offering relief from it changes the calculation. The method: ask one question whose answer you already know (to establish that you are informed, not ignorant), then ask the question you actually want answered. People give more to the second question because they believe it is a small increment from what you already know. They are managing a disclosure they assume is already partially made.

On success: the NPC gives you accurate information but may omit details they assume you already have. Ask follow-up questions about what was not said; silence around a topic tells you as much as speech.

The error to avoid: starting with the question you actually want. That tells the NPC exactly where your ignorance is, which gives them control over what they reveal. Start from the perimeter and move inward.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>DC 17 Charisma (Persuasion) — Negotiating with a tribal leader who has no reason to cooperate and every reason to distrust you</strong></summary>

A Germanic chief's authority rests on his ability to appear strong and perceptive to his followers. Anything you say to him that he must visibly consider is a gift to his authority; anything that makes him look surprised or unsure is a cost to it. The correct approach: give him something he can present to his followers as evidence that Romans treat him as worth talking to. This means using his title correctly, acknowledging his specific victories rather than making generic compliments, and making your request in terms of his interest rather than yours.

The specific thing that does not work: appealing to Roman law or Roman authority in a context where he has no obligation to respect either. He knows he has no obligation. Stating it gives you nothing and confirms that you are operating from a framework he has already rejected.

What does work: offering something he can demonstrate to his council. Information he does not have, a Roman product he cannot otherwise access, a favor that will be visible to the people who evaluate his leadership. A chief who gains something tangible from talking to you has a reason to talk to you again. DC 17 Charisma (Persuasion); on success, you establish a basis for continued communication. On failure, you have told him more about your situation than he has told you about his.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>DC 14 Charisma (Performance) — Using military ceremony to change the emotional state of a frightened group</strong></summary>

Military ceremony has a specific effect on soldiers who are frightened: it replaces individual fear with collective identity. A party member who performs a recognizable ritual during a crisis (raising a standard, calling formation, beginning the morning salute) can use DC 14 Charisma (Performance) to shift a panicked group to frightened and a frightened group to alert and functional.

This works because ceremony addresses the social and psychological function of collective action, not its religious function. A god does not need to be listening for it to work. The soldiers do need to be watching.

Conditions required: at least one recognizable military symbol must be present (a standard, a weapon held formally, a specific uniform element). The performance must be initiated by someone who appears to be in command. The group must share the ceremonial reference: Roman soldiers respond to Roman ceremony; Germanic allies respond to their own forms. A Roman ceremony performed in front of Germanic warriors has no mechanical effect.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>DC 13 Charisma (Intimidation) (Optio only — active: addressing soldiers who are refusing an order under fire) — The specific words</strong></summary>

There is a specific form of address that Roman military doctrine provides for soldiers who have stopped under fire. It is not a threat. It is a reminder: "You are soldiers of Rome. Rome is watching what you do here." The power is not in the words; it is in the fact that soldiers who hear it are reminded that this moment will be reported, that someone will say what they did or did not do, and that the accounting happens in Rome, not in this forest. A soldier's reputation follows him. The Optio who uses this knows it works not because of discipline but because of pride. DC 13 Intimidation; on success, the refusing soldiers return to the line for this encounter. On failure, they hold their position but do not advance.

</details>


## Poisons, Medicine, and Field Healing

*Ability check: Intelligence (Nature) or Wisdom (Medicine)*

You have watched the *medicus* work. If you have served long enough, you have held someone still while he worked. You know what a wound going bad looks like -- the smell is the first sign, before the discoloration and before the fever -- and you know that the difference between a man who survives a stomach wound and one who does not is partly luck and partly how fast the *medicus* gets there. Soldiers share practical knowledge: yarrow stops bleeding, willow bark reduces fever, the white mushrooms by the creek are fine and the red ones will kill you by morning. None of this is medicine. It is the minimum. Actual medicine is what the *medicus* does, and you watch him do it and you remember, because on a bad day you may need to do it yourself.

**What you know without a check:**

<details>
<summary><strong>Medicine proficiency</strong></summary>

Wound fever signs before they become obvious to non-specialists (the smell change, the specific quality of elevated skin temperature, the eye response); the field hospital triage hierarchy (dying vs. treatable vs. walking wounded) and what each category actually means in resource allocation terms.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>Herbalist's Kit proficiency</strong></summary>

Yarrow, willow bark, and hemlock by sight, smell, and texture in the field; the difference between a foraging kit assembled for cooking and a kit assembled for medical or other purposes; which plants in this region are dangerous regardless of quantity.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>Capsarius role</strong></summary>

You make the triage decision under fire, which means you have made peace with something most soldiers have not: the correct choice is not always the most morally satisfying one. A soldier with a survivable wound who has stopped fighting costs the battle more than a soldier with an unsurvivable wound who keeps fighting until he cannot. You prioritize the wounded by their ability to return to action, not by the severity of their suffering. This is doctrine. It is also the thing that combat medics do not discuss in peacetime, because peacetime medicine runs differently. The Capsarius's triage decision is always correct; the difficulty is explaining it afterward.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>Medicus role</strong></summary>

Plague wounds behave differently than normal wounds during plague season. The specific fever pattern before rash appearance is a 24-72 hour window during which infected soldiers are already contagious but show no visible signs. A Medicus who knows what to look for in that window can identify plague exposure before the unit is compromised. The early signs: a specific pattern of sweat-timing (heavy sweating in mid-afternoon rather than during exertion), a slight yellowing at the corners of the eyes, and an unusual craving for cold water. None of these individually indicate plague. All three together, in an otherwise healthy-appearing soldier, indicate the early window.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>DC 13 Wisdom (Medicine) — Recalling field hospital procedure, common medicines, wound infection signs, and poisoning recognition</strong></summary>

The Roman military maintains a *valetudinarium* (field hospital) at any permanent installation. The standard approach to wounds: clean the wound with wine or vinegar (which reduces infection without anyone understanding why), remove foreign material, bandage firmly. Cauterization for wounds that will not stop bleeding. Amputation for limbs that cannot be saved.

Common field medicines: *theriac* (a compound antidote used for general poisoning, snake bites, and as a general protective), willow bark preparation (reduces fever), honey as wound dressing (antiseptic properties), and various herbal preparations depending on what is available locally.

Soldiers know the practical signs of a wound going wrong: fever, swelling beyond the immediate wound, red streaks moving from the wound site, the particular smell that means the flesh is dying. Any soldier who has seen enough field medicine can recognize these signs, even without knowing the underlying cause.

Poisoning signs that a soldier might recognize: sudden collapse after eating or drinking, convulsions, skin color changes (pale, blue, flushed), excessive salivation, loss of consciousness. The soldier's instinct is to check whether others who ate the same food are affected.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>DC 15 Intelligence (Nature) or Wisdom (Medicine) — Recalling plant-based medicines, the dose-poison threshold, and the praegustator system</strong></summary>

Specific plant-based medicines available in the Germanic frontier region: yarrow (*Achillea millefolium*, named for Achilles who used it to treat wounded soldiers) for wound healing; *opium* (poppy preparation) for severe pain management; hemlock in careful doses as a muscle relaxant; *belladonna* in very careful doses for pain; *henbane* for sedation during surgical procedures.

The line between medicine and poison is quantity. Hemlock that treats muscle spasm in small doses kills in large ones. *Belladonna* that reduces pain in small doses causes delirium and death in larger ones. A trained *medicus* knows the thresholds. An untrained person making preparations from the same plants is likely to miscalculate.

Poison identification: the smell and appearance of certain preparations. Hemlock has a distinctive mousy smell. Aconite (*wolfsbane*, highly toxic) leaves a tingling sensation in small amounts that a taster might notice. Lead acetate (sweet, used as a sweetener in Roman cooking, gradually accumulates to toxic levels) has no obvious immediate effects.

The Roman practice of food-tasting: wealthy and powerful Romans employed tasters not out of paranoia but as sensible precaution given that poisoning was a real political tool. The *praegustator* ate a portion of every dish before the patron ate. This protected against fast-acting poisons; it did nothing against slow accumulation.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>DC 17 Intelligence (Nature) — Recalling expert poison craft: aconitum method, cicuta signatures, and the Lex Cornelia legal exposure</strong></summary>

*Aconitum* (wolfsbane) was the preferred assassination tool in Rome for a generation after the Julio-Claudian period. It was popular for a specific reason: it can be introduced into wine without affecting the taste, symptoms begin 30 minutes to two hours after ingestion, and it leaves minimal trace. Tingling in the mouth, then difficulty swallowing, then cardiac arrest. By the time a *medicus* examines the body, it looks like a bad heart. The reason it fell out of fashion is that it became better known among physicians. A *medicus* who has seen one case can now identify the next one.

*Cicuta* (hemlock) is slower and more available, but the visible convulsions make the cause obvious to anyone who has seen it before. It is the poison of someone who is willing to be caught, or who does not know better.

The law that governs this: the *Lex Cornelia de sicariis et veneficis*. Possessing poison preparation without a medical context is a capital offense. Roman law distinguishes *venena bona* (medicines in therapeutic doses) from *venena mala* (the same substances used against a person). The distinction is the intent, not the substance. A character carrying wolfsbane without Valeria's authorization is, in legal terms, carrying evidence of attempted murder. Keep this in mind.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>DC 15 Wisdom (Medicine) (Medicus only — active: examining any soldier who has been near the vault excavation for more than four hours) — Vault exposure versus corruption onset</strong></summary>

The vault's environment affects the body in specific ways that mimic early-stage plague symptoms. The cold damp air creates the sweat pattern; the organic smell creates the eye yellowing; the low-light extended period creates the water craving. A Medicus who examines vault workers can distinguish between vault-exposure symptoms and early plague. This is important in Session 1: after the spear is retrieved, several soldiers near the vault will show symptoms. The Medicus can determine whether this is environmental (vault exposure) or divine (corruption beginning). The distinction changes the treatment protocol.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>DC 13 Wisdom (Medicine) (Capsarius only — active: treating any wound in the northeast barracks near the spring) — The spring's coagulant property</strong></summary>

Wounds in this specific location heal faster than expected. Not dramatically: roughly 20% faster than standard tissue repair. The Capsarius notices this because they track healing progress and it is measurably off. The cause is the spring water's mineral content, which has a mild coagulant property. This is a practical advantage: patients in this wing of the barracks can return to duty one day sooner than standard recovery. The Capsarius is the only one who will notice this without someone pointing it out, because they are the only person who tracks healing rates.

</details>


## Reading Divine Signs

*Ability check: Wisdom (Insight) or Intelligence (Religion)*

Every Roman soldier watches three things without being taught to: where lightning falls relative to the camp, which direction the wolf ran when it crossed your path, and whether the sacred fire at the altar was burning or out at first light. These are not superstitions. They are data points. The gods communicate through the physical world, and they always have. The question is whether you are paying attention. A crow on your left when you leave the gate is not nothing. Whether it matters depends on what you are about to do and how seriously you take the relationship. Most soldiers pay enough attention to notice, then make a judgment call. The ones who ignore the signs entirely tend to become cautionary examples.

**What you know without a check:**

<details>
<summary><strong>Religion proficiency</strong></summary>

The augury bird system by reflex (right is favorable, left is not; eagles favorable, owls ambiguous, ravens unfavorable; wolf direction relative to the camp); the three basic categories of *haruspicina* that any observer picks up from watching enough sacrifices.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>Wisdom 14+</strong></summary>

You notice sign-patterns that others let pass as coincidence. You know when a day feels wrong before anything has happened -- a quality of light, a stillness, the behavior of animals. You have learned to pay attention to this. You have not always been right but you have been right often enough.

</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>Haruspex role</strong></summary>

You read signs under pressure differently than you read them in calm. The fear response sharpens some perceptions and dulls others: under pressure, you see more blood detail and less environmental detail, because your body is primed for immediate danger. You have learned to compensate by deliberately slowing your breathing and looking away from the most obvious sign to see what is in your peripheral vision. A Haruspex who uses this technique can read omens correctly in combat or crisis conditions that would compromise a less-trained diviner.
